text.p: The fraternity among golfers was never more evident. Seve Ballesteros was hitting balls on the practice range with Greg Norman standing right behind him, offering advice.
The two, one currently the world's top player, the other a former holder of that distinction, played together in a special six-man challenge on Tuesday ahead of Thursday's Dubai Desert Classic.

Then Norman went with Ballesteros, the Ryder Cup captain who admits he is low on confidence after missing the halfway cut in his only two tournaments this year, to the driving range as the Spaniard continued his long search for the missing ingredient in his game.
"We all hate to see a good player going through a bad spell," the Australian explained on Wednesday.
"Seve's too good a player to be playing in confusion the way he is.
"He's got too much talent, it's just a matter of him putting the right key in the door and when he has unlocked it he'll be off and going again."

Ballesteros, the winner of five major titles who struggled with his form for all of last year, showed his erratic side again on Tuesday by visiting several bunkers and hitting into the lake at the last hole.
"It's really just talking to him and then letting him figure it out for himself," said Norman of a player who is notoriously reluctant to take advice.
"Like I said to him yesterday, 'if you free up your swing, you'll free up your mind'.
"Just a simple statement like that might help him out."
While Ballesteros languishes now in 127th place, Norman continues to hold the top spot despite a three-month break from the game since he won his fifth Australian Open title in November.

"I needed to rest my back and get away for a while from what I have been doing for the past 20 years," Norman said. "I've never taken that much time off but it's been great and I'll definitely do it again."
The break enabled him to concentrate on his considerable business interests, which include golf course design, clothing and a forthcoming restaurant chain.
"I was going into the office every day at eight o'clock and staying until four in the afternoon," he said.
The course design work is burgeoning while his clothing line is also a huge success.
"I spend a lot of time on the design of the clothes, on fabric and quality because I think that side of the business might be good for generations," he said.
He took time out after Christmas to prepare for the finals of the Andersen Consulting World Championship of Golf, where he won the title and the jackpot of one million dollars.
"I did some work for that because I figured if I was going to play I didn't want to play like an idiot.
"Besides there was a pretty good incentive to play well," he said of his winnings.

The Australian multi-millionaire made a late decision to play in this week's Desert Classic, in a field which also includes Spaniard Jose Maria Olazabal, back after 18 months of foot problems, European number one Colin Montgomerie, Ian Woosnam and Bernhard Langer.
"I felt I needed some rounds under my belt before playing next week in the Doral Open (in Florida)," he said.
It is his first European Tour appearance, except for the British Open, since he played here two years ago.
But he disclosed that he will also play in the Spanish Open in May -- again because of the Ballesteros connection.
"Seve asked my nine months ago to play in it. I haven't played there since I played the European Tour full-time."
That was back in the late 1970s.
